did_you_know.text: Did you know? In this chapter, Jerusalem is portrayed as a speaking, human figure, and the prophet is commanded to tell her about her abominations. This literary device emphasizes her moral responsibility.

Did you know? Jerusalem is symbolically described as the daughter of a Hittite mother and an Amorite father. This is not necessarily a genealogical description, but rather a portrayal of foreign and flawed origins within a prophetic allegory.
Did you know? Jerusalem is told twice, “In your blood, live!” The repetition emphasizes her deliverance and her transition from abandonment and the threat of death to life and growth.

Did you know? The covenant between the LORD and Jerusalem is described in the language of marriage: the LORD spreads his cloak over her, covers her nakedness, and swears an oath to her. In this way, the covenant is presented as both protection and commitment.

Did you know? After the LORD gives Jerusalem clothing, jewelry, and food, she becomes famous for her beauty and even “succeeds to royalty.” Yet the text emphasizes that all her splendor came from the gifts the LORD gave her.

Did you know? One of the chapter’s most serious accusations is that Jerusalem sacrificed her sons and daughters to idols. In doing so, she turned the lives the LORD had given her into offerings to false gods.

Did you know? The chapter presents an unusual reversal of the image of prostitution: Jerusalem does not receive payment, but pays others to come to her. This reversal highlights the depth of her dependence on foreign alliances and foreign worship.

Did you know? Jerusalem’s judgment is described as having her deeds brought back upon her head: the nations to which she turned gather against her, destroy her high places, and strip her of her symbols and possessions.

Did you know? According to Ezekiel, Sodom’s sin included pride, material prosperity, complacency, and abundant food, along with indifference toward the poor and needy. The verse therefore emphasizes that her guilt was social and moral, not merely religious.

Did you know? Despite Jerusalem’s breaking of the covenant, the LORD says that he will remember the covenant of her youth and establish an “everlasting covenant” with her. The purpose of restoration is for her to remember her ways, be ashamed, and know that he is the LORD.
